title: My levels are generated from photos, and the explorable part turned out to be the size of a closet. How would you design exploration in 4 m²?
author: Key-Obligation-1065
selftext:
I'm designing a gentle first-person puzzle game where each level is generated from a photo. What the camera saw counts as real, and everything past the frame was invented by a world model. The plan was expeditions: head out into the invented part, recover pieces of the photo the dream scattered there, and bring them home.

Then I measured my first generated worlds. The invented floor you can actually walk on is about 4 m², and nothing is more than 5 m from where the photo was taken.

The rules, at least, still fit in a room. The invented part is light, so you jump higher there. Carrying a recovered piece makes you heavy, because its light restores reality, gravity included. Ghostly dream bridges are solid only inside that light. And the dream gets sizes wrong, so a giant teacup is a platform until you restore it. Float across a gap to the lamp, find you're too heavy to float back, then walk home across a bridge that only exists because of what you're carrying.

The open question is the expedition part. A meter that fills while you're far from anything real only creates tension if far means something, and in a room it barely does.

Would you lean into vertical space, tune the meter so even short trips matter, or treat each room as one dense puzzle?

Repo: [github.com/MichaelYeh507/Unpictured](http://github.com/MichaelYeh507/Unpictured)
